m.description: Number of distinct item sizes (item types)

b.description: Number of items (demand) required for each item type

assumptions.description: There is at least one item type.
Every item size is a positive integer that does not exceed the bin capacity.

code.python: assert all(1 <= w[d] <= W for d in range(m))

assumptions.description: The demand for every item type is positive.

code.python: assert all(b[d] >= 1 for d in range(m))

J.description: Set of all valid cutting patterns: non-negative integer vectors (a_0,...,a_{m-1}) whose total width does not exceed the bin capacity

x.description: x_a denotes the number of bins cut according to pattern a = (a_0,...,a_{m-1}) in J

constraints.description: The full demand of every item type must be satisfied by the chosen patterns.
constraints.formulation: \sum_{a \in J} a_d x_a \geq b_d \quad \forall d \in \{0, \ldots, m-1\}

constraints.description: The number of bins cut according to each pattern is non-negative.
The total number of bins used across all patterns doesn't exceed the total number of items.

code.gurobipy: model.addConstr(gp.quicksum(x[a] for a in J) <= sum(b))

objective.description: Minimize the total number of bins (patterns) used.

code.gurobipy: model.setObjective(gp.quicksum(x[a] for a in J), GRB.MINIMIZE)

notes: This is the classical Gilmore-Gomory pattern (cutting-stock) formulation, Equations (1)-(4) of carvalho1999, with the set of valid cutting patterns J defined by Equations (5)-(6). carvalho1999 treats J as an implicit, typically astronomically large set generated by column generation rather than enumerated up front; because this dataset requires a fully self-contained MILP, `J` is instead computed directly as a definition by enumerating every non-negative integer vector satisfying (5)-(6), which is tractable at the small scale of this dataset's instance.

carvalho1999 Proposition 2.1 shows the LP relaxation of this model is equivalent to the LP relaxation of the arc-flow model of formulation `c` (via Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition), and the source explicitly identifies path/pattern formulations such as this one as the 'classical formulation' that formulation `c` reformulates.
The source does not exclude the trivial all-zero pattern from J; we follow it literally. It is a redundant column (it satisfies no demand) and is never used in an optimal solution.

The total-usage bound (sum_{a in J} x_a <= sum(b)) is not present in carvalho1999's Equations (1)-(6); it is added here because the demand constraints are inequalities (>=), so without an upper bound the total number of bins is otherwise unbounded above (e.g. arbitrarily many copies of any single valid nonzero pattern remain feasible even after demand is met). The bound never excludes an optimal solution, since an optimal packing never uses more bins than there are items.
